content: Leukoplakia refers to patches that develop on the tongue, inside the mouth, or on the inner surface of the cheeks as a response to chronic irritation. These patches can also form on the external female genitalia. The symptoms of leukoplakia typically include sores that most commonly appear on the tongue but may also be found on the inner cheeks or external female genitalia. Hairy leukoplakia, a specific subtype, is characterized by painless, fuzzy white patches on the sides of the tongue. The sores associated with leukoplakia are usually white or gray, though they can sometimes appear red (a condition known as erythroplakia, which carries a higher risk of progressing to cancer). These lesions are thick, slightly raised, and have a hard surface that cannot be easily scraped off. Leukoplakia primarily affects the mucous membranes of the mouth. While it is often attributed to irritation, the exact cause is not always clear. Potential sources of irritation include rough teeth, irregular surfaces on dentures, fillings, or crowns, as well as smoking or other forms of tobacco use, particularly pipe smoking. Holding chewing tobacco or snuff in the mouth for extended periods can also contribute. Hairy leukoplakia, a distinct condition, is most commonly observed in individuals who are HIV-positive. It may be one of the earliest signs of HIV infection and can also occur in people with weakened immune systems, such as those who have undergone bone marrow transplants. Hairy leukoplakia is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, though the condition itself is not harmful. The disorder is most frequently seen in elderly individuals. The characteristic white patches of leukoplakia develop gradually over weeks to months. Over time, the lesions may become rough in texture and sensitive to touch, heat, spicy foods, or other irritants. A biopsy of the lesion is necessary to confirm the diagnosis. Examination of the biopsy specimen may reveal changes indicative of oral cancer. It is important to seek medical attention if you notice any lesions resembling leukoplakia or hairy leukoplakia. The primary goal of treatment is to eliminate the lesion. Addressing the source of irritation is crucial and may lead to the resolution of the lesion. This includes treating dental issues such as rough teeth, irregular denture surfaces, or problematic fillings as soon as possible. Smoking and the use of other tobacco products should be discontinued, and alcohol consumption should be avoided. In some cases, surgical removal of the lesion may be required. This procedure is typically performed in a healthcare provider's office under local anesthesia. Leukoplakia affecting the vulva is managed in the same way as oral lesions. Leukoplakia is generally harmless. Lesions often resolve within a few weeks or months after the source of irritation is removed. However, in rare cases, leukoplakia may progress to cancer. Preventive measures include quitting smoking and avoiding the use of other tobacco products. Alcohol consumption should be avoided or limited. Prompt treatment of rough teeth and repair of dental appliances is also recommended.
